ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Safe water to affected communities of chemical leak from Union Carbide in Bhopal 
*221. SHRI NANDI YELLAIAH: Will the Minister of CHE MICALS AND FERTILIZERS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Amnesty Secretary General while addressing the Prime Minister during 
2006, expressed deep concern that Government has fa iled to ensure regular and sufficient piped 
drinking water to all affected communities in Bhopal in compliance with a 2004 Supreme Court order, 
as several thousands of people in several parts of Bhopal still drink even today poisoned water, even 
after more than two decades, after the deadly chemi cal leak from the multinational Union Carbide 
Plant; and 
(b) if so, the details of action taken so far, by the Central and the State Governments? 
THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI RAM  VILAS PASWAN): (a) 
and (b) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) The Secretary General, Amnesty International had appealed to the Prime Minister in an 
open letter dated 6th April, 2006 to take immediate  steps to ensure regular supply of adequate safe 
water for the domestic use of the affected communities in Bhopal, in line with the order issued by the  
Supreme Court. 
The Supreme Court of India vide its order dated 7th May, 2004 directed the State Go vernment of 
Madhya Pradesh to ensure safe drinking water supply  to the 14 gas affected bastis situated near the 
Union Carbide Plant at Bhopal. 
The Government of Madhya Pradesh, in compliance with the orders of Supreme Court, 'ook action 
and installed 98 water tanks at different places in the said bastis. 
During the initial stage, these tanks were filled u p by transportation of water through private and 
Corporation tankers. As an interim measures, four t ubewells were drilled at Raslakhedi, which is five 
kilometers away from these bastis and two 50,000 gallon capacity sumps were constructed at Bhanpur 
and Blue Moon Colony. Remaining tanks are still bei ng filled by transportation of water through 
tankers. Water is being chlorinated and is potable and quality testing done regularly. 
Based on the sanction by Government of India in Apr il, 2006 for a project under the Jawaharlal 
Nehru National Urban Renewal Mission (JNNURM), the Government of Madhya

Pradesh had sanctioned Rs. 14.18 crore to Bhopal Mu nicipal Corporation (BMC), under this project, 
for providing safe drinking water through pipelines from the Kolar Reservoir to 14 localities around the 
UCIL plant site. The Government of Madhya Pradesh has informed that the work order amounting to 
Rs. 10.55 crores for laying and joining of the D.I.  pipes had been issued on 20th July, 2007 and Rs. 
2.74 crores for construction of R.C.C. overhead tanks issued on 6th November, 2007. Work related to 
these activities is under progress. Completion time  of these works, as informed by the State 
Government, is one year from the date of issue of work orders. 
In addition, a Consultant has been appointed for preparation of a Detailed Project Report (DPR) for 
distribution of water in Bhopal city, including the 14 bastis.

DR. K. MALAISAMY: Sir, it is most disheartening to note that the problem of drinking water 
supply to the victims of Bhopal gas blast is yet to  be solved. From the reply of the Minister we are 
able to see that the tragic event took place as early as two decades back and the Supreme Court order 
was dated 2004 and the letter of Amnesty Secretary General is 2006. From the facts we are able to see 
that the problem of drinking water supply is in the process of correction. They should have taken long-
term or short-term measures. As far as drinking wat er supply is concerned why should wait for the 
Supreme Court order? It is the basic responsibility of the Government and the local authorities to do 
these things. Sir, I would like to ask now whether they have taken it very seriously and whether they 
can give a time frame before which they can say that everything is complete as per the Supreme Court 
order.

has an opportunity to clarify for the convenience of the people as also for the sake of the media which 
has been criticising this issue and calling it a scam in the country. 
The first part of my question is whether the hon. M inister can convince this House that import of 
wheat was absolutely necessary. Secondly, in the Maharashtra Assembly, this issue

wheat which was imported and which was given to the  State of Maharashtra was unfit for human 
consumption. The question arises whether the hon. M inister accepts that part of the wheat that was 
sent to Maharashtra was unfit for human consumption. 
I would like to ask the hon. Minister, what action has been taken against the supplier of this wheat, 
whether proper compensation has been asked for, wha t is the amount of compensation the 
Government has received for such a type of wheat, and whether international law has been used in this 
particular case. 
SHRI SHARAD PAWAR: Sir, I would first like to make one position clear before the August House 
about this folly. When the orders were given, along  with the orders, quality norms were also provided 
for. When we have received the material from the various suppliers, there is a procedure that is followed. 
We do not straightaway accept the material that has  been brought into the country. There is an 
inspection by Health authorities. When the cargo arrives at the Indian ports, samples are drawn by the 
Health authorities, authorised under the PFA Act, u nder the supervision of the Customs authorities. 
The samples are tested at the public health laborat ories authorised by the Minister of Health, and in 
case the sample fails the test, we do not accept it. In this case, the stuff of each and every ship was tested 
by these authorities and they had accepted that it was up to the mark. There were three shiploads of 
material which were not up to the mark. One was rej ected by the Government and that Russian ship

of foodgrains in this country. It is a fact that it  was reported recently that most of the big busines s 
houses are entering into retail business and they are doing the procurement, and the FCI is lagging behind. 
So, a report to this effect was there. They were in the forefront. Half-a-dozen companies are there. Are 
we serious about it? Naturally, the peasant will se ll his product where he will get better price. That is 
happening, whether it is Punjab, Haryana or U.P. In this belt, the FCI is not in a position to collect its 
procurement. In such a situation, two things are th ere. One is that FCI has to do an aggressive 
procurement of foodgrains. Similarly, you have to enhance the MSP. Unless MSP is enhanced, how will 
the Government get the foodgrains? It is a fact tha t internationally, now there is a diversion of crop  
pattern from foodgrains to bio-fuels. So, the Government won't be in a position to import according to 
its demand. Seriousness on the part of the Government is required which is not reflected in the reply of 
hon. Minister. I want a categorical reply from the hon. Minister and an assurance to this august House on 
whether FCI will take up an aggressive procurement programme which will include enhancing of 
minimum support price for both, wheat and rice. Sir, agitations by the peasants are going on. What is the 
assurance which we are going to get from the Minister?

SHRI SHARAD PAWAR: Now, the highest rise has been g iven. Sir, an issue was raised as to 
why the procurement was not done by the FCI? Sir, p rocurement is always done with the help of 
the State Governments. 
From two States only, namely, Punjab and Haryana, out of 11 million tonnes, 10 million tonnes 
has been procured. From other major wheat producing  States like Uttar pradesh, Bihar, Madhya 
Pradesh, Rajasthan and Gujarat, we could not procure. I do-not want to go into details. I will give 
you some figures. 
Coming to Bihar, the total production was 35 lakh t onnes; total procurement was only 8,000 
tonnes, and, quantity of wheat supplied from the Government of India's kitty to Bihar was 17,50,000 
tonnes. So, they produced 35 lakh tonnes but they c ontributed only 8,000 tonnes towards the 
Government of India's kitty. 
Take the case of the State of Gujarat where the tot al production was 30 lakh tonnes; total 
procurement was zero, and, the supply from Government of India was 8,59,000 tonnes. Coming to 
the State of Madhya Pradesh, it produced 71,60,000 tonnes; procurement was only 57,000 tonnes 
and, the supply from the Government of India's kitty to Madhya Pradesh was 16,49,000 tonnes. As 
far as Rajasthan is concerned, the total production  was 69 lakh tonnes, total procurement was 
3,83,000 tonnes and the Government of India's supply to that State was 13 lakh tonnes. With regard 
to Uttar Pradesh, the total production was 259 lakh tonnes, total procurement was five lakh tonnes 
and the total material supplied by the Government o f India to the State of Uttar Pradesh was 27 
lakh tonnes. 
I have written to all the Chief Ministers. In such a situation, it is the responsibility of the State 
Governments also to cooperate with the Government o f India in the process of procurement, and, 
if the major producing States, except Punjab and Ha ryana, are not ready to cooperate with the 
Government of India for procurement, there will be problems of shortage. In such a situation, to 
resolve the problems relating to food security, the Government of India has no alternative to make 
arrangements whether it is within or outside.

14    Oral Answers               [RAJYA SABHA]                                   to Questions  
Prices of medicines 
†*223. SHRI PYARELAL KHANDELWAL: Will the Minister of CHEMICALS AND 
FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of steps being taken by the Government for controlling the prices of medicines and 
providing medicines on cheap/fair rate to the poor; 
(b) whether it is a fact that some medicines have been added and some have been removed by 
making changes at large scale in the control-list b y the Government for providing medicines at 
cheaper price; 
(c) if so, details thereof; and 
(d) the details of the efforts made by the Cabinet Comm ittee formed in this regard and the 
achievements made in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI RAM  VILAS PASWAN): (a) 
to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (d) The Government is committed to ensure th e availability of life saving drugs at 
reasonable prices. For this purpose, the Department  of Chemicals and Petrochemicals is taking 
various measures through National Pharmaceutical Pr icing Authority (NPPA). NPPA is ensuring 
availability of medicines at reasonable rates throu gh effective administration of provisions of Drugs 
(Price Control) Order, 1995 for Scheduled drugs and  through effective monitoring of prices in the 
case of Non-Scheduled drugs. Some of the steps take n by the Government and the NPPA to check 
the price rise and high prices of medicines are: 
1. Better market surveillance, detection and suo-moto scrutiny by NPPA has resulted in much 
better and effective enforcement of provisions of D PCO, 95. Because of better surveillance, 
the number of all first time price approvals in the  last two and a half years has been much 
higher as compared to previous years. About 65% of the total prices fixed by NPPA for the 
first time are during this period. 
2. As a result of better market surveillance, the NPPA  has undertaken frequent price fixations 
in the cases of Scheduled formulations. About 80% o f such price fixation were price 
reduction. 
3. The price rise in the case of Non-Scheduled formula tions is kept under check through 
effective monitoring on the basis of data from ORG- IMS. Government has delegated powers 
to the National Pharmaceuticals Pricing Authority ( NPPA) for fixation of prices of Non-
Scheduled formulations in "public interest" under p ara 10(b) of Drugs (Prices Control) 
Orders, 1995 (DPCO, 1995). Subsequent to delegation  of powers, NPPA have fixed prices in 
respect of 22 Non-Scheduled formulations under para  10(b) of DPCO, 95 between June, 07 
to October, 07 (List enclosed at Annexure). The del egation has facilitated in expeditious 
action by the NPPA to monitor and control the price s in case of price increases beyond the 
prescribed limit with respect in the cases of Non-Scheduled formulations. 
4. As a result of Government's efforts the pharmaceuti cal Industry has voluntarily agreed to 
reduce prices of 886 generic formulation packs. 
To make available life saving and essential drugs a t reasonable prices. This Department has 
prepared draft National Pharmaceuticals Policy-2006. The proposed policy contains

various measures to ensure better availability of d rugs at reasonable prices and better access to 
medicines for the people belonging to BPL families.  The draft National Pharmaceuticals Policy was 
considered by the Cabinet at its meeting held on 11 .1.2007. The Cabinet has referred the Policy to a 
Group of Ministers (GOM). 
The Government has recently approved a Health insur ance scheme namely "The Rashtriya 
Swasthya Bima Yojana", which is expected to cover a ll the BPL families in the unorganized sector 
in the next five years. The total sum insured would  be Rs. 30,000/- per family per annum and would 
cover the hospitalization expenses. The Government' of India would contribute 75% of the annual 
premium and the State Governments would contribute the remaining 25%. 
The 74 bulk drugs specified in the First Schedule o f the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 1995 
(DPCO, 95) and the formulations based thereon are u nder price control and their prices are 
fixed/revised by the National Pharmaceutical Pricin g Authority (NPPA) in accordance with the 
provisions of the DPCO, 95. Government has not made  any amendment in the list of bulk drugs in 
the First Schedule of DPCO'95 in the recent past. H owever, prices of several new formulation packs 
have been fixed by NPPA in public interest as per the enclosed Statement-I {See below). 
The Group of Ministers constituted to examine the D raft National Pharmaceuticals Policy, 2006 
has held two meetings on 10.4.2007 and 12.9.2007. T he Group of Ministers has discussed various 
issues related to the Pharmaceutical Industry with the officials of the Department of Chemicals and 
Petrochemicals, Representatives of Pharmaceutical I ndustry Associations and Representatives of 
consumer groups.

†*225. SHRI UDAY PRATAP SINGH: Will the Minister of  HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: (a) whether Government 's attention has been drawn towards spread 
of Japanese

Encephalitis in the eastern region of Uttar Pradesh, particularly in Gorakhpur and Basti Divisions; 
(b) if so, the number of persons who died on account of  this desease and the handicapped patients 
suffering from this disease; 
(c) whether Government's attention had also been drawn to such type of disease during the 
previous years; and 
(d) if so, the measures taken for prevention of this di sease and the measures being taken for 
rehabilitation of handicapped persons suffering from this disease? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBU MANI RAMADOSS): 
(a) to (d) Japanese Encephalitis (JE) is an outbrea k prone viral infection having cyclic trend with 
seasonal phenomenon. Children below 15 years are mo stly affected. Based on clinical systems, the 
cases are reported as case of Acute Encephalitis Syndrome (AES). 
During 2007 (upto 23.11.2007), the State Health Aut horities have reported 2450 cases of AES 
and 499 deaths in Uttar Pradesh. The test of 1477 c ases confirmed 147 as JE. The total number of 
handicapped patients identified in the State during  the year 2005 is 529. The number of handicapped 
patients during the years 2006 and 2007 is being identified. 
The following steps have been taken by the Central Government for prevention and control of 
this disease. 
* Standard guidelines for AES/JE surveillance has been disseminated. 
* 15 sentinel sites with laboratory support have been identified for pro-active surveillance. 
* JE diagnostic kits have been provided to the sentinel sites. 
* One Apex Referral Laboratory at SGPGI Lucknow has b een identified for advanced 
diagnosis. 
* A Vector Borne Diseases Control Surveillance Unit h as been set up at BRD Medical 
College, Gorakhpur, for field visits and for streng thening of surveillance activities with the 
financial assistance from Government of India. 
* To strengthen the Department of Microbiology in B.R .D. Medical College, Gorakhpur, one 
Microbiologist and one Lab Technician have been app ointed on contractual basis for the 
period of one year out of Government of India funds. 
* A Sub-office of Regional Office of Health and Fam ily Welfare, Lucknow, has been     
established and functioning in BRD Medical College Campus, Gorakhpur, since 2nd April,    
      2007. 
* Rapid response teams have been constituted in each JE endemic districts and trained. 
* Training courses for Microbiologists and Technician s of sentinel laboratories have been 
conducted. 
* Preparedness for prevention and control of AES/JE f or eastern U.P. is being reviewed 
regularly under the Chairmanship of Additional Director General and Director,

National Institute of Communicable Diseases, Govern ment of India, who is incharge of 
Disease surveillance in eastern UP, and meetings wi th the concerned officers/ experts of the 
Government of India, World Health Organisation, Sta te Government and ROH&FW are 
being held regularly. 
* JE vaccination campaign with live attenuated vaccin e in the age group of 1-15 years was 
launched in 2006. This campaign is being followed b y its integration in Universal 
Immunization Programme (UIP) covering new cohorts ( Children 1-2 years of age). 7 
districts of Uttar Pradesh viz. Gorakhpur, Deoria, Kushi Nagar, Maharajganj, Lakhim pur 
Kheri, Siddharth Nagar and Sant Kabira Nagar were c overed under JE vaccination campaign 
during 2006. In 2007, the JE vaccination was implem ented in 11 districts of Uttar Pradesh 
viz. Ambedkar Nagar, Behraich, Balrampur, Barabanki, Bas ti, Gonda, Mau, Rai Bareily, 
Saharanpur, Sitapur and Sravasti with 97% coverage overall. For 2008, the campaign has 
been planned for another 9 districts of Uttar Prade sh viz. Lucknow, Sultanpur, Hardoi, 
Muzaffarnagar, Azamgarh, Bareily, Ballia, Unnao and Faizabad. 
* The essential drugs and disposables for the managem ent of AES/JE cases are being supplied 
to the State Government. Supply of insecticides, la rvicides and bed nets for personal 
protections etc. is also made. 
* Close monitoring and supervision and periodic review is done regularly. 
* Multidisciplinary Central teams comprising of neuro logist, epidemiologist, microbiologist 
and entomologist have been visiting the districts s ince August, 2007. Based upon their 
observation and recommendation, control measures ha ve been stepped up. Since only 15% 
of AES cases are being diagnosed as JE, team from N ational Institute of Virology (NIV), 
Pune, took samples for detailed investigation and isolation of any other organism(s). 
* A field unit of NIV, Pune at BED Medical College, Gorakhpur, is being set up. 
* Improving cleanliness and sanitation in and around residential areas through activities to be 
undertaken by Village Health and Sanitation Committees under NRHM. 
As far as rehabilitation of handicapped persons suf fering from this disease is concerned, as the 
rehabilitation of handicapped persons is a State su bject, the State Government is taking actions as 
per their plans. But some of the actions which have  been specifically undertaken by the State 
Government, including some of the rehabilitation measures, are as follows: 
* Daily case reporting of AES cases is being continued. 
* Treatment of AES cases is provided in the Pediatric  Department of BRD Medical College 
and district hospital, Gorakhpur. 
* AES cases and deaths are verified in the villages. 
* Line listing of the cases is being done. 
* Vector control operations include fogging is being done in surrounding house of confirmed 
J.E. cases. 
* IEC activities for prophylactic measures and early cases reporting.

Sterilization performance 
*226. SHRIMATI SUPRIYA SULE: 
SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be p leased to state: 
(a) whether concerned over a decline of 4.3 per cent in  sterilization performance in the country, 
his Ministry has further enhanced the compensation package for loss of wages to people who adopt 
family planning methods and the compensation has be en doubled for men undergoing vasectomy to 
boost male participation in family planning; 
(b) whether this is the second revision within a year; and 
(c) if so, to what extent would this second revision he lp in implementing the family planning 
schemes? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBU MANI RAMADOSS): 
(a) and (b) A Statement indicating State/UT-wise st erilisation performance since the year 2002-03 is 
enclosed (See below). The performance of the sterilisation operat ion has shown a declining trend in 
the last few years inspite of provisioning of steri lization services free of cost at all public health  
facilities as well as involvement of the private ac credited facilities in the EAG States (Bihar, Uttar  
Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand, Orissa). 
Accordingly in October, 2006, the compensation pack age was revised from Rs. 400/- to Rs.800/- 
for EAG States for all categories and from Rs. 300/ - to Rs.800/- for tubectomy and Rs. 200/- to Rs. 
800/-for Vasectomy in Non-EAG States for Below Pove rty Line (BPL) acceptors only. Since this 
revision in the compensation package failed to reve rse the declining trend, the compensation 
package was further enhanced from 7th September, 20 07. In the current revision, the rates for 
Vasectomy has been increased from existing Rs. 800/ - to Rs. 1500/-(Rs.1100 is for acceptor) for all 
categories in all States and Tubectomy from Rs. 800 /- to Rs. 1000/- (Rs. 600 is for acceptor) to all 
categories in High focus States (Bihar, Uttar Prade sh, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Jharkhand, 
Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand, Orissa Jammu and Kashmir , Himachal Pradesh, Assam, Arunachal 
Pradesh, Manipur, Mizoram, Meghalaya, Nagaland, Tri pura, Sikkim) and BPL/SC/ST population in 
Non High focus States (Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nad u, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Goa, 
Gujarat, Punjab, Haryana, West Bengal, Delhi, Chand igarh, Puducherry, Andaman and Nicobar 
Islands, Lakshadweep and Minicoy Islands, Dadra and  Nagar Haveli, Daman and Diu) in public 
health facilities. However for APL categories in No n-High Focus state, a package of Rs. 650/- 
(Rs.250 for acceptor) has been provided for tubectomy only.

Compensation package has been enhanced to Rs. 1500/ - for both Vasectomy and Tubectomy in 
accredited private health facilities to all categor ies in High Focus States and vasectomy for all 
categories and tubectomy for BPL/SC/ST population in Non-High Focus States. 
(c) The Second revision will help in implementing t he family planning schemes in the following 
ways: 
1. Empower the clients, specially the rural poor to seek, access and avail of the services without 
having to bother about their loss of wages. 
2. Create a more enabling environment for the service providers like doctors, nurses, OT 
technicians, etc. 
3. The Enhanced compensation to doctors would also enc ourage them to get training in the 
sterilisation procedures to address the acute shortage of manpower. 
4. The increased compensation to all categories of mot ivators would lead them to motivate 
more cases of sterilisation. 
5. The increase in the compensation package to the acc redited private/Non-Governmental 
sector would bridge the gap of unmet need of family planning services. 
Along with the above modification, the other initia tives like strengthening of quality health 
delivery under NRHM, National Family Planning Insur ance Scheme, partnership with the non-
governmental sector, presence of Accredited Social Health Activists in villages, espanding 
contraceptive choice for family welfare, skill upgr adations and thrust on quality care will go a long 
way in achieving the goal of population stabilization.

Though Health is a State subject, the special focus  given to the Health Sector in the National 
Common Minimum Programme (NCMP), has formed the cor e of the programmes formulated under 
Health, Family Welfare and AYUSH. The National Rura l Health Mission (NRHM) is the key plant 
for giving effect to the mandate of the NCMP. Focus ed strategy to arrest HIV/AIDS, other 
communicable diseases and life style related diseas es is complementary to the strengthening of 
healthcare delivery system visualized under the Mission. 
National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) was launched i n April, 2005. The objective under the 
Mission is to provide health care facilities in the  rural areas of the entire country with special foc us 
in 18 States viz. 8 States with poor health indices  (Bihar, Jharkhand, M.P., Chhattisgarh, U.P., 
Uttarakhand, Orissa and Rajasthan), 8 North Eastern  States (Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, 
Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim and Tripura) a nd the hill States of Himachal Pradesh and 
Jammu & Kashmir. 
Under the NRHM, a wide range of policy initiatives have been taken for improving health 
infrastructure and address the health care needs of  the population to achieve better health indicators . 
The main aim of NRHM is to provide accessible, affo rdable, accountable, effective and reliable 
primary health care facilities, especially, to the poor and vulnerable sections of the population. It 
also aims at bridging the gap in Rural Health care services through creation of a cadre of Accredited 
Social Health Activists (ASHA) and improved hospita l care, decentralization of programme to 
district level to improve intra and inter-sectoral convergence and effective utilization of resources.  
The NRHM further aims to provide overarching umbrel la to the existing programmes of Health and 
Family Welfare including RCH-II, Malaria, Blindness , Iodine Deficiency, Filaria, Kala Azar, T.B., 
Leprosy and Integrated Disease

Surveillance. Further, it addresses the issue of he alth in the co ntext of sector-wide approach 
addressing sanitation and hygiene, nutrition and sa fe drinking water as basic determinants of good 
health in order to have greater convergence among t he related social sector Departments i.e. 
AYUSH, Women & Child Development, Sanitation, Eleme ntary Education, Panchayati Raj and 
Rural Development. 
For correcting regional imbalance in the availabili ty of affordable/reliable tertiary healthcare 
services and also to augment facilities for quality  medical education in the country, the Government 
has launched the Pradhan Maritri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana (PMSSY). Under PMSSY, six new 
AIIMS like institutions are to be set up and 13 medical colleges upgraded all over the country. 
Concerted efforts are also being made to arrest com municable diseases like HIV/AIDS and non-
communicable diseases like cardiovascular diseases,  diabetes, deafness, mental health etc. besides 
strengthening the existing national health programmes. 
Community participation and Decentralized Planning together with flexible funding is 
facilitating States to look at ground reality and p lan accordingly. Experience over the last two years  
shows that the NRHM is rapidly expanding in the cou ntry. Fresh initiatives being taken by the 
States as a part of this mission process will further strengthen the health delivery mechanism.

The average rate of soil erosion in the country is 16.4 tonnes per hectare per year. Out of total 
eroded soil, 61% simply moves from one place to ano ther, nearly 29% is lost permanently to the 
sea and remaining 10% is deposited in the reservoir s. The soil erosion leads to land degradation in 
upper reaches of the river system, whereas when dep osited at various locations of river system in 
the downstream, it may increase the soil fertility.  About 5.3 million tones of soil and around 8.40 
million tones of plant nutrients are displaced annu ally through water erosion. Rough estimate also 
show that agricultural loss from soil erosion vario us to the tune of Rs. 5200 — 8400 crore per 
annum in the country. 
Government of India is implementing various Watersh ed Development Programmes with a view 
to minimizing soil erosion, land degradation and th ereby sustaining agricultural production in the 
country. These programmes are: (i) National Watersh ed Development Project for Rainfed Area 
(NWDPRA), (ii) Soil Conservation for Enhancing the Productivity of Degraded Lands in the 
Catchments of River Valley Project and Flood Prone River (RVP&FPR), (iii) Reclamation of 
Alkali Soils (RAS), (iv) Watershed Development Proj ects for Shifting Cultivation Area 
(WDPSCA), (v) Drought Prone Area Programme (DPAP), (vi) Desert Development Programme

The Government of India has enacted the "Cigarettes  and other tobacco products (Prohibition of 
Advertisement and Regulation of Trade and Commerce,  Production, Supply and Distribution) Act, 
2003, mainly to discourage consumption of tobacco p roducts. Some of the important provisions of 
the act are: 
(i) Prohibition of smoking in a public place. 
(ii) Prohibition of direct and indirect advertisement of cigarette and other tobacco products. 
(iii) Prohibition of sale of cigarette and other to bacco products to a person below the age of 
eighteen years. 
(iv) Prohibition of sale of tobacco products near the educational institutions.

AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to  state what possible steps 
Government is undertaking to provide proper warehou sing facilities to farmers, so as to 
avoid the post harvest losses of the produce? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER A FFAIRS, FOOD AND 
PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (DR. AKHILESH PRASAD SINGH): Pr imarily, there are three 
Government agencies i.e. Central Warehousing Corporation, Food Corporation o f India and State 
Warehousing Corporations which are engaged in build ing storage/warehousing capacities for 
foodgrains which provides scientific storage facilities to avoid post harvest losses of the produce. 
The Central Warehousing Corporation (CWC) is having  adequate warehousing facilities 
throughout the country for storage of foodgrains to  avoid the post harvest losses of the produces of 
the farmers. As on 01.10.2007, it had 498 Nos. of G eneral Warehouses having total average 
capacity of 100.50 lakh MT and the average utilizat ion of 77.70 lakh MT. The total foodgrains 
stored in the warehouses of CWC were 25.68 lakh MT.  CWC offers a rebate of 30% in storage 
charges to the bona-fied farmers. It has launched Farmers Extension Service Scheme (FESS) 

Written Answers to             [30 NOV. 2007]                 Unstarred Questions   69 
since 1978-79 to educate farmer about the benefit o f Scientific storage and use of public warehouses 
and is also imparting training to the farmers on th e techniques of scientific storage and preservation  
of foodgrains so that storage losses at their level  are minimized and demonstrates the spraying and 
fiimigations methods to fanners to control insects and rodents. 
Although the FCI does not provide warehousing facil ities directly to the farmers yet, it constructs 
storage capacity at nodal points to manage the proc ured foodgrains stocks on central pool account. 
Concerned State Governments also construct godowns to provide warehousing facilities to the 
fanners at village, block, district and taluq level. 
The FCI holds adequate storage capacity all over th e country. As on 1.11.2007, total capacity 
held by the FCI is 239.67 lakh MT (151.47 lakh tonn es owned and 88.20 lakh tonnes hired from 
various agencies) which is sufficient at macro leve l. For micro level, space requirement, FCI has 
proposed to the Government of India for constructio n of about 4.00 lakh tonnes capacity in various 
States including the newly declared procurement Sta tes during the Eleventh Five Year Plan to 
successfully manage the procurements/maintenance of  adequate stocks for supplies in the Public 
Distribution System and other schemes. 
Besides above, another scheme for construction of r ural godowns for providing storage facilities 
in rural areas monitored by the Department of Agric ulture and Cooperation known as "Gramin 
Bhandaran Yojana" is also existing to enable farmer s to enhance their holding capacity to sell their 
produce at remunerative price. Government is provid ing subsidy @25% of the capital cost of the 
project. A higher subsidy of 33.33% of the capital cost is provided for beneficiaries belonging to 
SC/ST categories and for North Eastern States and H illy areas. Till 2007, a total of 17,099 rural 
godowns project with a total capacity of 200.96 lak h tonnes having subsidy component of Rs. 
577.00 crores have been sanctioned in the country. 
Under the National Policy of handling Storage and T ransportation of Foodgrains announced in 
June, 2000, private sector is being encouraged to b uild bulk storage capacities as per latest 
technology for storing foodgrains procured by Gover nment agencies which will lead to reduction in 
storage transit losses and ultimately benefit the f armers. Storage capacity to the tune of 5:5 lakh 
M.T. is presently being created under Build-Own-Operate (BOO) basis in the country.

1223. SHRI RAMDAS AGARWAL: Will the Minister of HEA LTH AND FAMILY

women aged 15- 49 and 15.9% of urban men aged 15-49  are overweight or obsese having Body

schemes through out the country which directly or i ndirectly improve the nutritional status of 
women and children. Some of these are as under:

Rural Health Mission (NRHM) in order to improve the availability

level to improve intra and inter-sectoral convergen ce and effective utilization of 
resources.

5 years and Iron & Folic Acid Supplementation for p reschool children, pregnant and 
lactating women. 
(b) Maternal Health care by promoting institutional del iveries, improved coverage and 
quality of Ante Natal Care (ANC), skilled care to p regnant women, Postpartum care at 
Community level. 
(c) Immunization services. 
(d) Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illnesses and malnutrition. 
(e) Emphasis on Infant & Yong Child Feeding. 
(iii) National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme.

nutrition.

(c) National Programme for Nutritional Support to Prima ry Education (Mid Day Meal

THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBU MANI RAMADOSS): 
(a) and (b) No such specific report has been brough t to the notice of this Ministry. However, a 
Monitoring Study of Pesticide residues and heavy me tals in vegetables available in Delhi market has 
been carried out by the All India Network Project o n Pesticide Residues, Indian Agriculture 
Research Institute, New Delhi. 
A total of 54 samples of various vegetables (bhindi , palak, tomato, parwal, bringal, cabbage) 
were collected from Agriculture Produce Marketing C ommittee (APMC), Azadpur, New Delhi and 
analysed for the possible residue of pesticides and  heavy metals, during the period of June 2006 to

and brinjal, residues of pesticide, namely cholrpyr ifos were detected which were below the 
prescribed Maximum Residue Limit (0.2 ppm) under PF A Rules, 1955. However, in rest of the 50 
samples, no pesticide residues were detected. 
As far as adulteration in food articles is concerne d it is stated that the implementation of the PFA 
Act, 1954 and Rules, 1955 is entrusted to the Food (Health) Authorities of the States/U.Ts. The 
enforcement staff of the Food (Health) Authorities draw samples of different food articles from all 
sources viz. Manufacturers, Wholesalers and Retailers and get th em analysed so as to see whether 
the samples conform to the standards laid down unde r PFA Rules, 1955 and other provisions of the 
PFA Act. 
As per the information made available so far by Food (Health) Authorities for the Annual Reports 
on the working of the PFA Act and Rules in their re spective State/U.T, the percentage of 
adulteration in different food articles has decline d from 11.71% in the year 2002 to 9.57% in the

Courts of Law respectively, against the offenders f or violating different provisions of the PFA Act,

Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 would get  repealed on coming into force of the Food 
Safety & Standards Act, 2006, under which different  penalties are envisaged for sub-standard, 
misbranded and adulterated foods which varies from Rs. 25000/- to Rs. 5,00,000/-. 
There are specific penalties for food which are uns afe and varies depending upon the gravity of 
offences, from an imprisonment for a term which may  extend to six month with fine which may 
extend to Rs. One lakh to a term for six years and fine which may extend to Rs. 5 lakhs. Where to 
contravention results in death, the punishment may extend to imprisonment for a term which is not 
less than 7 years but which may extend to imprisonm ent for life and also with a fine which shall not

intends to imrpove the performance of family welfar e services by reducing total fertility rate, 
maternal and infant morbidity and mortality, and un wanted pregnancies. Under NRHM & RCH-II, 
the Programme Implementation Plans of States inter alia include the action plan for family planning 
activities.

Recurrance of Chikungunya in Kerala 
1238. SHRI K. CHANDRAN PILLAI: Will the Minister of  HEALTH AND FAMILY

(a) whether Government is aware of the recurrance of diseases like Chikungunya in Kerala; 
(b) if so, whether Government has taken measures to combat the situation; 
(c) whether the existing facilities for diagnosing the diseases are inadequate in the State;

(a) Yes, Sir. The State of Kerala has been reportin g cases of Chikungunya fever since July, 2006 
onwards. During 2006, total 70731 and in 2007 till 31st October, 24030 suspected cases of 
Chikungunya fever have been reported. 
(b) and (c) 1. Government of India has prepared a L ong Term Action Plan for Prevention and 
Control of Chikungunya in the country and sent to the States including Kerala for implementation. 
2. For proactive surveillance Medical College, Kottaya m; Medical College, 
Thiruvanthapuram and Medical College, Kozikode with  laboratory support have been 
identified as Sentinel Surveillance Hospitals in the State. 
3. For advance diagnostic facility, Quality Assurance and capacity building, above Sentinel 
Surveillance Hospitals were linked with Kerala Stat e Institute of Virology and Infectious 
Diseases, Alapuzha which has been identified as Apex Referral Laboratory. 
4. Microbiologists and laboratory technicians of these  institutes have been trained on_ sero-
diagnosis. 
5. The supply of IgM ELISA test kits for diagnosis of Chikungunya to the identified 
institutes has been made through NationaUnstitute of Virology, Pune. 
6. To meet the operational cost, contingency grant of Rs. 50,000/- to each Sentinel 
Surveillance Hospital and Rs. 1.00 lakh to the Apex Referral laboratory has been released.

package during 2006-07 for purchase of Fogging Mach ines, Pyrethrum Extract (2%), 
Temephos, Insecticide treated bed nets and for cond ucting IEC activities. Similarly, during 
2007-08, Rs. 4.04 crore has been released for purch ase of Pyrethrum Extract (2%),

1244. SHRI SYED AZEEZ PASHA: Will the Minister of H EALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to ad vertisements running for the past few 
months on television for 7 carbonated beverage alongwith images of lemon fruit slices;

Statement 
Outcome of Independent evaluation of National Leprosy Eradication Programme by Indian Institute 
of Health Management Research, Jaipur (IIHMR)  
An independent evaluation of NLEP was carried out b y Indian Institute of Health Management 
Research (IIHMR), Jaipur during February - May' 05 to assess the programme achievement status at 
the close of World Bank supported Second National L eprosy Elimination Project. The study was 
carried out in 13 different endemic States. 
Following are the major findings of the study: 
The PR reduced from 3.74 in March 01 to 1.99 in Dec ember '04 a 47% reduction and ANCDR 
reduced from 5.6 to 3.1 (45% reduction). MB proport ion increased in almost all States and 
percentage of female in new cases increased from 35 .5 to 36.2%. Child percentage reduced in most 
of the States indicating success in controlling tra nsmision. The percentage of Grade - II disability i n

THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBU MANI RAMDOSS): (a) 
to (d) The findings of the Fourth Assessment of the  Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change 
(IPCC) are estimations of current scientific unders tanding of impacts of climate change on natural, 
managed and human systems, the capacity of these sy stems to adpat and their vulnerability. It sets 
out projected climate change related exposure likel y to affect the health status of millions of people , 
particularly those with low adaptive capacity through, 
• increases in malnutrition and consequent disorders,  with implications for child growth and 
development. 
• Increase deaths, diseases and injury due to heat waves, floods, storms, fires and droughts. 
• The increased burden of Diarrhoeal diseases, primarily associated with floods and droughts. 
• The increased frequency of cardio-respiratory disea ses due to higher concentrations of 
ground level ozone related to climate change, and 
• The altered spatial distribution of some infectious disease vectors. 
A multiple strategy, which includes mitigation, ado ption, technological development and research 
needs to be devised to diminish the risks associate d with climate change. Sustainable development 
can definitely reduce the vulnerability to climate change by enhancing adaption capacity and 
increasing resilience.

undertake surveillance, early detection and prevent ion and control of outbreaks of communicable 
diseases including diarrhea. 
A integrated approach has been initiated with Depar tment of Drinking Water Supply to provide 
the technical support to monitor the quality of dri nking water in different States so as to prevent 
occurrence of water-borne diseases. A contingency p lan to combat droughts and floods has been 
prepared by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and has been circulated to all States.

1279. SHRI S.M. LALJAN BASHA: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that almost all railway coache s have become defective and hard to operate 
locks inside; 
(b) what steps would be taken to make it technically po ssible to open doors from outside in times 
of accidents;

(e) whether outside help would be sought to improve the designs of railway coaches; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS ( SHRI R. VELU): (a) to (c) 
The railway coaches have latches on doors which are  locked from inside during the run of the trains, 
so as to provide safety and security to the travell ing passengers, and there is no proposal to make it  
possible to open from outside, the doors of running  trains locked from inside of coaches. These 
latches are regularly attended to and kept in worki ng order, and can be opened to facilitate 
evacuation of passengers in case of fire or any oth er event requiring such evacuation. To further 
facilitate such evacuation, coaches are also fitted  with emergency exit windows and additionally 
with vestibules in case of reserved coaches. 
(d) to (f) Indian Railway coaches are well designed , and have been continuously upgraded to 
improve passenger safety and comfort, by taking not e of technological developments and 
international norms, and by transfer of technology,  wherever necessary. Thus, Indian Railways have 
switched over from wooden body coaches to integral steel shell coaches having anti-telescopic 
features. The design of steel shell coaches has rec ently been upgraded to improve crashworthiness of 
coaches, besides induction of tight lock centre buf fer couplers to prevent climbing of coaches on top 
of each other in the event of collisions. Specifica tions of most of the furnishing materials used in 
coaches have also been upgraded with regard to fire  retardant properties, to provide adequate time 
for evacuation of passengers in case of fire.

Expansion plan for Rourkela Steel Plant 
1315. SHRI RAMDAS AGARWAL: 
SHRI RUDRA NARAYAN PANY: 
Will the Minister of STEEL be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that SAIL has rolled out a  major expansion plan for Rourkela Steel 
Plant to augment the capacity; 
(b) if so, what is the existing capacity per annum and the proposed expansion plan by 2010 
indicating the likely investment to be made; 
(c) whether this growth plan will help to boost employm ent opportunities and recruitment of 
locals; and 
(d) if so, the present employees strength of SAIL and e mployees likely to be recruited by 2007-
10? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STEEL (DR.  AKHILESH DAS): (a) and 
(b) Yes, Sir. The expansion of Rourkela Steel Plant  (RSP) has been approved "in-principle" by 
SAIL Board in May '07. The proposed expansion plan of RSP envisages increase of hot metal 
production from 2.12 million tonnes per annum (2006 -07) to 4.5 million tonnes per annum at an 
indicative cost of Rs. 7,668 crores. 
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. Employment opportunities for qualified personnel will get a boost as 
recruitment of technical personnel, Diploma Holders  and ITI certificate holders would continue to 
be carried out for meeting skilled manpower recruit ment in view of the modernization/expansion of 
RSP. Retraining, Redeployment and Multi-skill train ing will also help in meeting skilled/semi-
skilled manpower requirement from the existing empl oyees. In addition to direct employment 
generation, expansion is likely to create employmen t opportunity for the ancillary and other support 
industries in the region. 
It may be relevant to mention that while Corporate Plan envisages enhanced production level by 
expansion/modernization of steel plant, it simultan eously lays emphasis upon achieving higher 
labour productivity, manpower rightsizing through n atural separations and VR and selective 
recruitments. As such the total manpower strength o f SAIL after capacity expansion is likely to be 
less than the present manpower strength of 130419 a s on 1.11.2007. While rationalization would 
continue further to increase competitiveness, simul taneously selective recruitments shall be 
undertaken to meet skilled manpower requirement for new projects/modernization. 
Accordingly, for meeting manpower requirement for n ew projects/modernization and existing 
facilities, provision is made in the recruitment pl an under the Annual Human Resource Planning 
(HRP). Under the Human Resource Plan for 2007-08, t he recruitment plan of SAIL is 3260 out of 
which 250 recruitments are allocated for RSP.

Revival of M/s. Bharat Heavy Plates and Vessels by way of its take over by BHEL 
SHRI TAPAN KUMAR SEN (West Bengal): Sir, I rise to draw the attention of the House and 
the Government to the news of recent Cabinet approv al to the financial restructuring of the premier 
public sector engineering company, M/s Bharat Heavy  Plates and Vessels Ltd., BHPV at 
Vishakhapatnam which I could learn from the release  of the Press Information Bureau dated 26th 
November, 2007 from the PIB website. The package en visages writing off and waiving off the loans 
and liabilities of BHPV by the Government of India,  and take over of BHPV by BHEL, and an 
investment of Rs. 275 crores by BHEL in BHPV. That is a good news. But, thereafter, certain 
disturbing incident has taken place. The concerned press note of 26th November, 2007 has been 
silently withdrawn from the Press Information Burea u's website, and now, it is in the air that the 
issue of writing off of loans and liabilities by th e Government of India for BHPV has been reopened 
again, and the matter would be renegotiated between  the Ministry of Heavy Industries and the 
Ministry of Finance. On inquiry from the PIB, we ca me to know that the release was withdrawn by 
instructions from above. I urge upon the Government  to clarify as to why and under what 
circumstances the PIB release dated 26th November, 2007 has been silently withdrawn. The manner 
in which it has taken place, lacks transparency and  smacks of a conspiracy. When the private sector 
takes over a sick public sector unit, all its loans  and liabilities are waived off and the Government 
grant huge concessions besides, handing over that s ick public sector company almost free of cost. 
But when a healthy public sector unit takes over a sick public sector unit, on that, the loans and 
liabilities are sought to be imposed on the healthy  public sector unit who is taking over. So, this is  a 
very bad practice and the manner in which the whole  thing was handled, smacks of a conspiracy 
against the most healthy and ideal practice taken u p by the UPA Government, that is, revival of sick 
public sector PSU by another healthy public sector PSU in view of the huge fund position of the 
healthy public sector unit from with in I want a cl arification as to why that PIB release was 
withdrawn from the website and whether the Cabinet approval announced by the PIB on 26th 
November, 2007 will be implemented by the Governmen t. That assurance I want from the 
Government.

GOVERNMENT BILL 
The Rajiv Gandhi Institute of Petroleum Technology Bill, 2007 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MUR LI DEORA): Sir, I 
move: 
"That the Bill to declare the institution known as the Rajiv Gandhi Institute of Petroleum 
Technology to be an institution of national importa nce and to provide for its incorporation and 
matters connected therewith, be taken into consideration" 
Sir, the Government introduced the Rajiv Gandhi Institute of Petroleum Technology Bill, 2007 in 
the Rajya Sabha on 7th September, 2007. 
I would like to apprise the hon'ble Members about t he need of setting up of Rajiv Gandhi 
Institute of Petroleum Technology and its declarati on as the "Institute of National Importance". The 
year 1999 witnessed the advent of the New Explorati on Licensing Policy, which has been 
progressively made more and more attractive. This p olicy has evoked great enthusiasm among 
foreign companies as well as Indian private and pub lic sector companies for acquiring exploration 
acreages in India. As on date, only 30% of the sedi mentary basins in India has been explored. It is 
planned to increase the exploration coverage to an extent of 100% by the year 2015. In this context, 
apart from technology, availability of adequate num ber of qualified personnel would be a prime 
requirement in the coming years. 
Sir, in a recent study conducted by consultant Pric ewaterhouse Coopers for Petrofed, it is 
estimated that the gap between the availability and  requirement of trained manpower in the field of 
Petroleum Technology in India would be about 3600 b y the year 2019. To substantially meet the 
shortfall of trained manpower in the petroleum sect or, it has been decided by the Government to set 
up Rajiv Gandhi Institute of Petroleum Technology (RGIPT) at Jais, UP. 
The institute is designed to serve as the fountainh ead for the nurturing of world class technical 
human resources capable of serving as the leaders a nd innovators of tommorow in the field of 
Petroleum Technology. To start with, the Institute will commence its academic operations by 
admitting students in basic undergraduate courses f rom the academic year 2008-09, from a rented 
campus. On its becoming fully operational the Insti tute world have 7 B.Tech, 6 Integrated Masters 
Degrees, 8 M. Tech/MBA and 12 PGD and Ph. D. programmes. 
The total estimated capital cost of the project is Rs. 435 crores which would be met partially 
through budgetary support of Rs. 285 crores and Rs.  150 crores from Oil Industry Development 
Board. The total estimated recurring expenditure of  Rs. 260.58 crores would be met from the accrual 
of interest on Endowment Fund of Rs. 250.00 crores to be created 

Government               [30 NOV. 2007]                  Bill    181 
with the contribution of Oil Public Sector Undertak ings (PSUs), student fees, donations and others 
earnings of the Institute. The Institute is envisag ed to be self-sufficient by the year 2015-16. It is  
proposed that RGIPT would have a high degree of aut onomy in terms of its academic, 
administrative and financial functioning. RGIPT wou ld have legal empowerment in its own right to 
enable it to grant degrees and other academic disti nctions and titles. Furthermore, it is envisaged th at 
RGIPT would enjoy the patronage and support of the Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas of 
Government of India. It is in the interest of the n ation that the Government nurture the institute in its 
nascent and crucial stage of development to enable the Institute to launch and run its programmes 
without compromise and set up world-class infrastru cture while offering courses of a high standard, 
in the absence of the status of the "institute of N ational importance", it would not be possible to 
attract eminent faculty members and meritorious students. 
In view of the proposed mode of establishment of RG IPT as outlined above, it is proposed that 
RGIPT be incorporated as an "Institute of National importance" through an Act of Parliament having 
a governance structure as well as legal empowerment  to grant degrees in a manner similar to that 
enjoyed by the IITs.

SHRI TAPAN KUMAR SEN (West Bengal): Mr. Vice-Chairm an, Sir, I thank you for 
having given me the opportunity. At the outset, I w ill, definitely, compliment the hon. Minister of 
Petroleum and Natural Gas for bringing forward this  Bill which envisages establishment of an 
Institute of national importance, for increasing th e number of technologically competent people in 
the petroleum technology, particularly, the explora tion technology in the country, of which there is a  
serious shortage. While complimenting this, let me also say that it is a belated step. Around 1970, 
the country's dependence on petroleum import was ab out 30 per cent. Now, I think it is 70 per cent 
plus. The way the demand of petroleum is increasing , vis-a-vis the petroleum being produced within 
the country, the dependence on petroleum imports is  going to increase much more in the fututre. It 
will go beyond 6ontrol. Steps to produce petroleum on a war-footing basis within the country need 
to be taken. It is not an impractical proposition. Many other countries which do not have petroleum-
reserves, that is, reserves of natutal resources, t hey can't dream of it; they have to depend on impor ts. 
But, geologically, it has been proved that we have much more reserves which we are yet to exploit 
and produce petroleum. So, in that situation, India  is having a very great potential, India is having 
immense potential for increasing its capacity to pr oduce fuel inside the country, to produce this vita l 
energy within the country. But our infrastructure, our manpower is not yet ready to take up that big 
challenge. So, in that situation, this effort of br inging up an Institute to increase the technologica l 
manpower of the country in the concerned field is a  good step. However, it is belated. But better late  
than never. It is welcome. 
The second point that I would like to suggest is, w hile the Institute of Petroleum Technology will 
be in place, we must stress more on exploration sid e and also on the refining side. There should be a 
balanced approach on both the sides. Why I am sayin g this is because if we see the problem being 
faced even in refining. Sir, the old refineries in our country are also facing problem vis-a-vis the 
latest refineries that have been set up in our coun try with updated technology. The main point is to 
take care of the additional sulphur content in the petroleum in the process of refining and also to 
keep the cost of refining within limit so that we c an produce the refined petroleum both imported 
and domestically-produced in a cost-effective manne r. In these areas also, there is dearth of enough 
technological manpower, technical manpower in the f ield of chemical engineering, in the fields of 
geological and metallurgical engineering. So, in th ese areas also, we have dearth of manpower and, I 
think, with this general engineering degree, they o ught to also specialise, focus on the refining 
technology area as well. We must also promote resea rch and development in these areas. I think, the 
Institute should also give due importance to the R& D work in fine-tuning the refining technology 
which we do have. We do have indigenous technology in our command to make it fine tuned, to take 
care of composition of the imported crude and to re fine it at the least cost, so that the petroleum ca n 
be made available to the people at a cheaper rate. So, this area is also needed to be given due 
importance in the Institute's curriculum, and, on t hat also, I give my humble suggestion to the hon. 
Minister. 
Sir, I think there is not much to be told, but the third point that I would like to make is this. As i s 
clear from the Bill and also from the finding of th e Standing Committee, the shortage is very high. 
As is mentioned in the Statement of Objects and Rea sons, — the hon. Minister also mentioned it 
while introducing the Bill — there is a shortage of  36,000 personnel. But,

Sir, the Minister should have given a break-up as t o how much shortage is there in the exploration 
side and how much shortage is there in the refining  side. So far as the exploration side is concerned,  
after NELP, newer fields are coming under explorati on and that area also is getting more priority in 
the days to come. So, the break up of the shortage also needs to be looked into in deciding the 
number of seats in different wings, exploration tec hnology side and also refining technology side. 
So, that also has to be looked into in deciding the  number of seats in the concerned areas. But in 
spite of whatever number of seats a single Institut e like this can ensure, the problem of shortage wil l 
still remain because the demand for the enough-petr oleum-technology-competent people will 
increase. It is not only in India. As per the Repor t, India is supplying technologically-competent 
persons in this field for the entire Asia. That is a reality. Sir, we will produce students. But the 
moment they will get the offer of a fat salary from  abroad, they will go out. So, the purpose will not  
be served. So, there should be creation of enough p ersons and, for this purpose, one Institute is not 
sufficient. Keeping that in view, I must compliment  the hon. Minister again. The Bill contains a 
provision in section 10 which provides that the Ins titute can also establish campus and academic 
centres in different parts of the country. One Inst itute cannot meet the demand that is coming in a 
big way, particularly after the Sixth Round of NELP . More and more fields are being brought under 
exploration. At the same time, the pressure on the refining sector has also been increasing. That 
cannot be managed by just one Institute. So, I thin k, the provision is there in the law. While 
supporting the Bill wholeheartedly and while wishin g it all the success, I also request the hon. 
Minister and, for the matter, the Government of Ind ia, to expedite the process simultaneously 
establishing campus and academic centres in differe nt parts of the country. An Institute will be there  
at that particular place. At the same time, the Ins titute must plan and open campus and academic 
centres in different IITs throughout the country gi ving priority to the petroleum-rich areas in the 
country, particularly in the eastern part, in the N orth-East, in the southern part in the Cauvery-
Godavari basin, as also in the western part of the country. Keeping that in mind, they must create 
campuses. 
My last point is that the Institute is going to be funded from the Budget by the petroleum PSUs 
and from the OID funds. Its control, its leadership  should also be tuned in that direction. We are 
setting up an Institute by spending so much money f rom the public exchequer. It should be for 
public good. So, it should be controlled by a publi c body, not a private body. That also must be 
ensured. And for that also, protection should be given. 
With these suggestions, I again support the Bill and thank the hon. Minister.

SHRI SHARAD ANANTRAO JOSHI (Maharashtra): Thank you , Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir. The 
proposer of the Bill has proposed, in fact, one and  a quarter ideas. One idea is to make voting 
compulsory, and a quarter idea, which has, incident ally, been inserted in a paragraph is about 
prohibiting the polls either before the voting or a fter the voting. Sir, it is an excellent idea, and it 
should have met with no opposition whatsoever. But,  the proposer being what he is, he tends to give 
rather than a sugar-coated quinine, a quinine-coate d sugar pill. There used to be a Finance Minister 
at the time of the Chinese aggression who had an ex cellent idea of collecting some money by way of 
deposits from the people. When the Chinese aggressi on took place, people were anxious to 
contribute to the national cause. But he called the  scheme, Compulsory Deposit Scheme. It was this 
word, 'compulsory', which gave lot of happiness to that particular Finance Minister, but, the scheme 
did not work as. well as he expected it would. Simi larly, I think, a good idea is being put in a 
quinine-coated pill by saying that it should be mad e compulsory. I would come to the first part of it;  
the compulsory voting part of it. 
Sir, the analysis made by all the previous speakers  is very correct. Firstly, the people, who get 
into the voters list themselves, are around 50 per cent and not more than that. There are quite a 
number of-people who do not figure in the list at a ll. And, there are quite a few people who always 
complain; particularly, even the celebrities compla in that their names are not included in the list. L et 
us say, 60 per cent of the people are included in t he voters list. Out of that the proportion of voter s 
can be 25, 35,40 or 50, so, we have got just about 30 per cent of the total citizenry which is voting.  
According to the first past the post rule, a person  who has even lost the deposit can get elected. Tha t 
has happened in many cases. But there are many case s where people who get ten per cent of the 
votes get elected. So, if you find out, then, techn ically, there is a possibility that a person, who d oes 
not represent even one per cent of the citizenry, g ets elected. Now, that is a situation which needs t o 
be corrected, and the proposer of the Bill, certainly, needs to be complimented for this reason. 
The important thing is, when he says the word, 'com pulsory', there are certain ramifications that 
follow. When you make it compulsory, do you undertake to see that every citizen,

notification appears in the newspapers, the courts have given clear judgement that the fact that it ha s 
appeared in the newspapers cannot be taken as suffi cient notice. Similarly, the fact that his name, 
actually, appears in the voters' list, cannot be ta ken as sufficient notice that the person knows that  
his name is there in the voters' list. There will b e an additional obligation on the part of the Elect ion 
Commission, or, the Returning Officer there to indi vidually intimate to every voter that his name is, 
actually, there; you simply can't say that the vote rs' lists are presented somewhere, you can go and 
find out. That will be an obligation, which will ha ve to be carried out if you make voting 
compulsory. This is number one. 
Number two, the remedy has to be done with a certai n amount of study. It is a fact that very few 
people like to go and vote. But if you make an anal ysis, you will find that there is a qualitative 
difference between the people who come to vote and those who don't come to vote; there is a class 
difference. And, as Misraji mentioned, the voters f rom the slum areas, from the poorer quarters, 
come and participate in a much larger proportion th an those who are well-to-do, who live in flats in 
cities. What is the reason behind this? Why is it t hat those who are relatively well-to-do are not 
interested in exercising their right to vote? I thi nk some analysis is necessary. I would say, Sir, th at 
after 60 years of exercise of electorate democracy,  there is a general apathy in the electorate and 
among the citizens that whatever the results of the  election, it does not really change the situation of 
the country as a whole. The people, at large, have given up the hope that any Party, any leader, will 
come into power who will, ultimately, bring about s ome change of significance for the country as a 
whole. The people who go to vote are, generally, th e people who expect some kind of a personal 
betterment as a result of the results of election. For example, there is some very prominent person in  
the slums who is able to tell those persons that un less they vote for a particular Party or a particul ar 
person, they will not be able to live in this slum.  This is the largest majority of people who, actual ly, 
come to vote. Consequently preparation for election  these days really means being able to purcahse 
these dadas. Sir, the other people who are relatively well-to-do  find themselves disinterested in the 
elections. The important thing is how can we make t he people who are better off relatively interested 
in the elections. Well, there can be a better way. If you say 'compulsory', then there is going to be a 
certain expenditure, even though that expenditure h as not been mentioned. And, our experience up 
till now is, everytime you try to enforce a reform,  then the police machinery comes in and, 
ultimately, it results in an additional burden on t he police machinery and increase corruption in the 
police machinery. Not only that, it also results in  the general slackening of the law and order 
situation. Sir, in this particular case, it will be  worthwhile finding out if it is the Income-tax pay ers 
who are, generaly, apathetic to coming to the polli ng booth and if some kind of an inducement be 
given. It is for the Finance Minister to make concr ete proposals as to whether some kind of an 
inducement can be given as there is an inducement g iven to the slum dweller that he will be able to 
live in the slums, or, at least be alive if he. vot es and he may not be alive if he doesn't vote. 
Therefore, a similar kind of inducement can be give n. Today, the element of compulsion and 
coercion is being exercised by the dadas of the slums; that is why, when people talks of aam admi, 
they are really talking of the mechanism which is u sed for rallying these people. Sir, as for 
compulsion, I would like to even ask a question: what is going to be

As regards the quarter part about not having the pr e-poll or post-poll results, I think, there is some 
kind of a drafting mistake. The idea possibly was n ot to ban or to prohibit the polls. The idea was to  
ban or prohibit the publication of the poll results , and there is a lot of difference between the two.  
You can't stop people from gathering information. T hat is his right of information. They have every 
right to collect knowledge. You can't stop me from going and trying to find out who has voted for 
whom. The only thing you can say is that he should not publish it in order to influence the trend of

correction in the Bill that it is not the polls tha t are being prohibited; it is the publication of th e polls, 
and once that correction is made, the question aris es, are you really opposed to the present kind of 
statistical polls or polls based on random sample, or, are you opposed to the publication? 
Sir, I know of a very prominent leader who used to be once a Cabinet Minister and he appears on 
the television and gives interviews. He gives his v iews about what is going to be the likely outcome 
of the elections that are forthcoming. He doesn't b ase himself on the electoral polls at all. But he h as 
such a reputation for being a wise man, knowing the  Indian polity, that his world has come to have a 
certain prestige and reputation. Now, are you going  to say that such predictions and such interviews, 
which are not based on any polls — he doesn't even claim to have a sample poll — will be allowed? 
Will that be allowed? 
And, let me say one more thing, Sir, that most of t he people don't go by pre-polls. A far more 
dependable prediction is given by the people who ta ke the satta on it. Even today if you want to 
know what is going to happen in Gujarat, then don't  go by any of the poll predictions, take it from 
what is the bet being given, and you will find that  in 95 per cent of the cases, it is the rate that i s 
given on the satta which comes out to be more dependable. Now, what wi ll happen is, that the satta 
will become more dependabel than the so-called pseu do-scientific polls. I am not claming that they 
are entirely scientific. There is nothing like an e ntirely sceintifc sample study, but rather than hav e 
that kind of an attempt an a scientific prognosis, if you encourage entirely unscientific, personal an d 
subjective prognosis, I don't think that will be an  improvement. In any case, you cannot prohibit 
polls, you will have to prohibit the publication of  the poll outcome, and if you want to prohibit the 
publication of poll outcome you have to make it celar that no kind of prediction, no kind of guess, no
